title: Two ongoing conditions on one pet can mean paying the excess twice, not once
excerpt: Most pet policies charge the excess per condition, per year — so a pet being treated for two separate issues can trigger two separate excesses in the same policy year.
body: Car and home insurance usually charge one excess per claim. Pet insurance often works differently, and it's easy to assume it works the same way until a vet bill proves otherwise: many policies charge the excess per condition, per policy year — not once overall, however many things your pet is being treated for.

In practice, that means a dog being treated for both a skin allergy and a knee injury in the same year could face the excess twice — once against each condition — even though it's the same pet, the same policy, and the same twelve months. Some insurers also add a co-payment percentage on top of the excess for older animals, which stacks on top of this per-condition structure rather than replacing it.

This sits alongside a separate distinction worth knowing: whether the policy is lifetime, time-limited, or maximum benefit. A lifetime policy resets its claim limit every renewal, which is the only type that reliably keeps covering a long-term condition year after year — but the per-condition excess still applies within that, condition by condition.

Before buying, it's worth checking two numbers rather than one: what the excess actually is, and whether it applies once per policy year or once per condition per year. For a pet with (or likely to develop) more than one ongoing issue, that second number can matter as much as the price of the premium itself.

If insuring more than one pet, it's also worth confirming any multi-pet discount applies per policy rather than per claim — a similar case of the fine print working differently to how the headline discount sounds.
